On the 1914 map, British Protectorate is the coast and hinterland of southern Arabia, from Aden east through the Hadhramaut toward Oman, held by local sultans under British protection.

Britain took the port of Aden in 1839 to guard the sea route to India. After the Suez Canal opened in 1869, Aden became a busy coaling station. To shield it from the Ottoman Empire, which held the north of Yemen, Britain signed treaties with the sultans and sheikhs of the interior. They kept their own rule, while Britain handled their foreign affairs. This was the Aden Protectorate.

It was protection on the cheap: few British officials, little money and indirect rule through local rulers. The same method bound Muscat and Oman and the sheikhs of Trucial Oman. The southern protectorates later became South Yemen in 1967; see Yemen under Britain.
